In low-NFE regime, it is generally known that deterministic samplers paired with well-tuned time discretization lead to better performance. To investigate the tradeoffs for Sigma -3B, we choose two representative tasks (GSM8K and HumanEval), and vary the sampler (DDPM or DDIM) and the time-discretization across various diffusion sampling budgets T ∈ { 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 , 64 , 128 , 256 } T\in\{4,8,16,32,64,128,256\} . Using the same optimal hyperparameters from the two tasks, we evaluate the 16/32-step performance across all six tasks in Tabs. 1 and 2 ; Tab. 8 shows performance at other budgets. 5.2 Embedding Regularization We observe that during training, embeddings collapse to ~4 effective dimensions in terms of principal components—a phenomenon not typically seen in standard autoregressive language model embeddings. While the current model achieves strong high-NFE performance, we hypothesize that regularizing the embeddings to be more uniformly distributed on the unit sphere will improve low-NFE performance. Our intuition is that representation collapse exacerbates token ambiguity, particularly when coarse numerical precision and low-NFE sampling introduce prediction errors. To mitigate this, we apply Sketched Uniform Spherical Regularization (SUSReg, Nicollier et al. (2026) ) to the embedding matrix 𝐄 {\mathbf{E}} during pre-training, penalizing the deviation between its empirical distribution and a uniform distribution on the unit sphere (see Sec. E.1 ). Results. As shown in Figs. 7 and 8 , the resulting Sigma -SUSReg-3B improves few-step and distillation results compared to Sigma -3B. Interestingly, SUSReg brings nearly no penalty to the validation PPL, although the learned embedding geometry differs substantially from that learned without SUSReg ( Fig. 8 ). 5.3 Parallel Decoding Distillation for Few-step Generation Although DDIM has better performance than DDPM at reduced denoising steps, the pretrained model still loses quality at very low NFEs with a clear drop-off below 16 NFEs ( Fig. 7 ). We therefore distill the many-step trajectory of Sigma -3B into a few-step student. Our method adapts Parallel Decoding Distillation (PDD, Shaul et al. (2026) ) to blockwise continuous language diffusion, see App. I for full details. Due to the parallel nature of the student PDD heads, they cannot utilize recurrent computation, so we distill from the teacher without self-conditioning (-SC). During distillation, we amortize CFG into our student by training the single conditional student call to match the two-call guided teacher directly, which reduces FLOPs during sampling. Results.
